summary: Defines the PPP encapsulation scheme for carrying multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links, together with the Link Control Protocol, an extensible way to negotiate link options. It was replaced by RFC 1548.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP is the way two computers agree to talk over a direct line, like a phone modem. First they settle the rules, then they send their data wrapped in a standard envelope.

questions: what is the link control protocol
what is the ppp frame format
subtitle: The original standard way to send IP and other network traffic over a plain serial link, with a built-in negotiation protocol.

tldr.problem: Point-to-point serial links were common, but there was no agreed Internet standard for encapsulating datagrams on them, and each vendor used its own scheme.
tldr.mechanism: PPP wraps each datagram in an HDLC-style frame with a protocol field, and uses the Link Control Protocol (LCP) to negotiate options, authenticate the peer and close the link, while Network Control Protocols configure each network-layer protocol.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1331 was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFCs 1171 and 1172 and was itself replaced by RFC 1548.

today: RFC 1331 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1548, so it is no longer the current PPP specification. It had itself replaced RFC 1171 and RFC 1172.

sections.title: Why PPP Exists
sections.content:
Most Internet hosts of the time sat on LANs or wide-area networks, and relatively few used simple point-to-point serial links, partly because no encapsulation protocol had been agreed upon as an Internet Standard. The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) fills that gap with three parts: a method for encapsulating datagrams on serial links, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) for establishing, configuring and testing the link, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) for configuring each network-layer protocol.

PPP runs over bit-oriented synchronous links and asynchronous links with 8 data bits and no parity. The links MUST be full-duplex but may be dedicated or circuit-switched. It builds on HDLC and can carry several network-layer protocols at once over the same link. By default only 8 additional octets are needed for the encapsulation, and it can shrink to as few as 2.

The design aims at easy configuration: defaults should cover common cases, and each end tells the other its capabilities through an extensible option negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers connected by a single wire needed a common way to wrap their messages. PPP is that wrapper plus a short chat at the start where they agree on the rules.

sections.title: The PPP Frame
sections.content:
A PPP frame uses the HDLC layout: a Flag (binary 01111110, 0x7e), an Address field that is always 0xff (all-stations), a Control field of 0x03, a two-octet Protocol field, the Information field, a 16-bit Frame Check Sequence (FCS) and a closing Flag. PPP assigns no individual station addresses.

The Protocol field says what the Information field carries. Values must be odd, with the low bit of the first octet equal to zero. Values 0xxx to 3xxx identify network-layer protocols (for example 0021 for IP), 8xxx to bxxx identify their NCPs (for example 8021 for the IP Control Protocol), 4xxx to 7xxx are for low-volume protocols without an NCP, and cxxx to fxxx are link-layer control protocols (c021 is LCP, c023 PAP and c223 CHAP). New numbers MUST be obtained from IANA.

The default maximum length of the Information field is 1500 octets, and other values can be negotiated. On asynchronous links the RFC's appendix defines a character-stuffing scheme using the Control Escape octet 0x7d.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message goes into an envelope with a start mark, a label saying what kind of message it is, the message itself, and a check number at the end to catch damage.

sections.title: Link Phases
sections.content:
A PPP link moves through distinct phases. It starts in Link Dead until the physical layer is ready. In Link Establishment, LCP exchanges Configure packets; the link is open once a Configure-Ack has been both sent and received, and non-LCP packets in this phase MUST be silently discarded. An optional Authentication phase follows: by default none is needed, but if one is negotiated, the link MUST NOT advance until the peer authenticates, and on failure PPP SHOULD go to Link Termination.

In the Network-Layer Protocol phase each network protocol such as IP MUST be configured separately by its NCP, and each NCP may be opened and closed at any time. Finally, in Link Termination, LCP closes the link with Terminate packets, after which the implementation SHOULD signal the physical layer to disconnect. Closing one NCP is not by itself a reason to end the link.
sections.plainLanguage: The link goes through steps like a phone call: the line comes alive, the two sides say hello and agree on rules, they may check who is calling, they talk, and then they hang up.

sections.title: The Option Negotiation Automaton
sections.content:
Negotiation is driven by a finite-state automaton shared by LCP and the NCPs. It has ten states (Initial, Starting, Closed, Stopped, Closing, Stopping, Request-Sent, Ack-Received, Ack-Sent and Opened). Events include the lower layer going Up or Down, administrative Open and Close, Restart timer expiry, and receiving the various LCP packets. Actions include sending Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak/Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack, Code-Reject and Echo-Reply. The simplified diagram is not complete: implementations MUST follow the full state transition table.

The link is Opened when both ends have sent and received a Configure-Ack. A Restart timer drives retransmissions; it MUST be configurable and MAY default to three (3) seconds. Max-Terminate should default to 2 transmissions, and Max-Configure and Max-Failure to 10. The RFC warns that two ends with conflicting policies may never converge, so implementors should add loop detection or higher-level timeouts.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side keeps track of where it is in the conversation, like a checklist: asked, answered, agreed. A timer makes it ask again if nobody replies.

sections.title: LCP Packets
sections.content:
Each LCP packet has a one-octet Code, a one-octet Identifier that matches requests with replies, a two-octet Length, and a Data field. It travels alone in the Information field of a frame with Protocol c021. There is no version field; a future version would use a different Protocol value.

Link Configuration packets are Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak and Configure-Reject. A Request lists the options a side wants; an Ack copies them back unchanged; a Nak lists only the unacceptable options with acceptable values suggested; a Reject lists options that are not recognized or not negotiable. Terminate-Request and Terminate-Ack close the link. Link Maintenance packets are Code-Reject for unknown codes, Protocol-Reject for unsupported protocols, Echo-Request and Echo-Reply for testing both directions, and Discard-Request, which the receiver simply throws away.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides send short notes: I would like these settings; fine; not quite, how about this; no thanks; goodbye. There are also notes for checking the line works.

sections.title: LCP Configuration Options
sections.content:
Options have a Type, a Length and Data. Anything not listed in a Configure-Request keeps its default, and unless stated otherwise an option applies to one direction only. The options defined here are Maximum-Receive-Unit (default 1500, and an implementation MUST still accept 1500 octet frames), Async-Control-Character-Map (default all ones, so all control characters are mapped), Authentication-Protocol (PAP or CHAP, default none), Quality-Protocol (default none), Magic-Number, Protocol-Field-Compression and Address-and-Control-Field-Compression.

The Magic-Number is a random number each end picks to detect a looped-back link. If a received number equals the one just sent, a Configure-Nak with a different value is sent. A Magic-Number of zero is illegal. The two compression options let a sender omit constant bytes: the Protocol field can shrink to one octet and the Address and Control fields can be dropped, but never in LCP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The options are the settings the two sides can tweak, such as the biggest message they can take. One setting is a secret random number each side sends so it can tell if it is accidentally talking to itself.

items.label: Configure-Request
items.desc: Proposes options to open the link.

items.label: Configure-Ack
items.desc: Accepts all options in the request.

items.label: Configure-Nak
items.desc: Refuses some option values and suggests acceptable ones.

items.label: Configure-Reject
items.desc: Refuses options that are unrecognized or not negotiable.

items.label: Discard-Request
items.desc: Data sink for testing; the receiver throws it away.

items.label: Async-Control-Character-Map
items.desc: Which control characters must stay mapped.

items.label: Protocol-Field-Compression
items.desc: Sends the Protocol field in one octet.

items.label: Address-and-Control-Field-Compression
items.desc: Omits the constant Address and Control fields.
